3d:Tfdc,## What happens

Warm-pool entries whose container has died stay `running` forever, hold their node slot, count against the node's allocation, and make that node permanently undrainable.

Measured on production 2026-08-06 by diffing `docker ps -a` on all nine nodes against the rows that claim them:

| | |
|---|---|
| real agent containers | 169 |
| rows claiming a container | 238 |
| **rows claiming a container that does not exist** | **77** |
| containers with no row at all | 8 (3 up since 13 July) |

Three autoscaled ccx33 nodes bought on 26, 27 and 28 July (`167.233.20.85`, `178.105.77.91`, `88.198.118.204`) hold **four such rows each**, have **zero containers**, and have read as fully allocated for ten days.

## Why nothing collects them

`WarmPoolManager.healthCheck()` probes every ready pool entry and destroys the dead ones — container *and* row, via `destroyPoolContainer` → `deleteAgent` → `deletePoolEntry`. It is exactly the missing collector, and it has **no live caller**: the only one is `/api/v1/cron/pool-health-check` on the container-control-plane, which the daemon's own comments call deprecated. The daemon's `runInfraMaintenanceCycle` runs node-health, disk, alloc-reconcile, pre-pull, autoscale, pool-drain, pool-replenish and orphan-reconcile — no pool health check.

This is the same omission as `replenish`, already documented in `provisioning-worker.ts` fifteen lines away, and nothing else can see these rows:

- **the heartbeat skips them.** `listRunning()` filters `execution_tier != 'shared'`, and `createPoolEntry` never sets `execution_tier`, so every pool row falls to the schema default `shared` — while carrying a real `node_id` and `container_name`. The docblock's premise ("shared rows are container-free by design") is false for pool rows.
- **`reconcileUnclaimable` cannot reach them.** Its candidate query ends `NOT (warmPoolRuntimeReadyConditions)` — a fully ready row is excluded by construction.
- **the orphan reconciler cannot reach them.** It starts from the Docker listing, so an empty node yields an empty candidate set.

## Why it costs servers

- `countAllocatedWorkloadsOnNode` counts non-terminal rows; `running` counts. The node reads as allocated.
- `findDrainCandidates` skips any node with `allocated > 0` — a row is treated as proof of a workload. The node can never be drained.
- `syncAllocatedCounts` runs every five minutes, armed, and re-asserts the inflated count rather than repairing it.
- `container-billing` and `agent-billing` select on `status = 'running'` with no node-side check, so **these rows are billed hourly**.

Net effect: the pool can only grow. Every phantom permanently removes a slot from `totalAvailable` and permanently disqualifies its node from drain.

## Related, not fixed here

- **The 77 rows already stranded** need the reverse reconciler — "row claims container C on node N, `docker ps` does not list it past a grace window → release the placement". No such path exists: every writer of `node_id`/`container_name` to NULL (`executeSleep`, `retireFailedWarmClaimForRetry`, `trySetProvisioning`) is triggered by a job or an error string, never by container absence.
- **`ORPHAN_RECONCILER_ENABLED` is set in no deployment config**, so the container-side reconciler has never run. It would collect the 8 rowless containers. Arming it is an ops decision — it issues `docker rm -f`.
- **`/v1/admin/docker-containers/audit`** — the ghost-container detection route — is a `501` stub.
- **`admin-infrastructure.ts` already computes the drift** and raises a `critical` alert past |2|. The three empty nodes sit at −4, so three critical alerts have been rendering for ten days with no remediation arm.
- **`processDisconnectedRecovery` is scoped `dedicated-always`**, so a `dedicated-lazy` row that flips to `disconnected` is never re-probed and holds its slot permanently — a second, quieter leak.
- **Node `capacity` looks wrong**: the autoscaler buys ccx33 and declares them 4 slots while the original nodes declared 24 are carrying 38.
3e:T1de0,## Summary

Following the contribution skill exactly — fill the repository template's
`contribution-attribution` rows, then append the eliza.army footer — produces a PR
body whose **machine marker is rejected by the scoring validator**. The
declaration that carries `client` and `skill_revision` is dropped, and the PR is
credited only with the weaker visible declarations (both `client: null`,
`skillRevision: null`). Coverage falls from `complete` to `partial`.

Both gates are individually satisfied. It is their combination — which the skill
instructs and CI enforces — that fails.

## Mechanism

`src/lib/leaderboard.ts` (elizaOS/army@`753f8446`, the deployed validator) counts
attribution footer lines across the **whole body**:

```ts
const providerModelLines  = attributionLineValues(body, "AI provider/model");
const clientLines         = attributionLineValues(body, "Client / agent tooling");
const skillRevisionLines  = attributionLineValues(body, "(?:Contribution skill revision|Skill revision)");
const statusLines         = attributionLineValues(body, "Attribution status");
if (providerModelLines.length !== 1 || clientLines.length !== 1 ||
    skillRevisionLines.length !== 1 || statusLines.length !== 1) {
  return "marker requires exactly one complete visible attribution footer";
}
```

`.github/pull_request_template.md` (develop, lines 32–37) ships three of those
four label texts as **mandatory** rows:

```
<!-- attribution-row:client -->
- Client / agent tooling: `client-name` / `None - human-only contribution`
<!-- attribution-row:skill-revision -->
- Skill revision: `owner/repo@full-commit-sha:path` / `N/A - no contribution skill used`
<!-- attribution-row:status -->
- Attribution status: `self-reported`
```

`scripts/check-pr-agent-attribution.mjs` requires every one of
`REQUIRED_ATTRIBUTION_ROWS = [ai-assistance, models, client, skill-revision, status]`
to be present with a concrete value, so the rows cannot simply be deleted — that
turns the PR gate red. And the skill states the rule that pairs them:

> fill the contribution-attribution row in the repository template and append
> this footer after the template.

Filling the template puts `Client / agent tooling:`, `Skill revision:` and
`Attribution status:` in the body; appending the footer puts
`Client / agent tooling:`, `Contribution skill revision:` and `Attribution
status:` in it again. Each count is 2, the marker is rejected, and the strong
declaration is lost.

The issue templates already carry the instruction that avoids this.
`.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/bug_report.md` tells reporters to add the marker as the
final body lines and **"Do not repeat the visible rows."** No such sentence
exists in `.github/pull_request_template.md`, and the skill's PR instruction says
the opposite — fill the template row *and* append the footer.

## Every arrangement was measured

Same PR body, four variants, all with the repository CI gate green
(`evaluatePrAttribution(body).findings === []`):

| PR body | scorer verdict |
| --- | --- |
| template rows + full footer (what the skill instructs) | `marker requires exactly one complete visible attribution footer` — partial |
| template rows + lane signature + marker (the issue template's rule, applied to a PR) | same reason — partial |
| template rows + marker only | `marker requires exactly one terminal lane signature` — partial |
| template rows with **relabelled** rows + full footer | `machine-marker`, client captured, **complete** |
| template provenance block deleted + full footer | `machine-marker`, complete — but the CI gate then fails |

So on the PR side there is no arrangement that follows the template's own label
text and keeps the marker valid. The only shapes that work either deviate from
the template's wording or drop rows CI requires.

## Reproduction

Against the shipped code on both sides, no reimplementation:

```
$ gh pr view 17749 --repo elizaOS/eliza --json body --jq .body > body.md
# scoring validator, imported from elizaOS/army@753f8446:src/lib/leaderboard.ts
assessModelAttribution([{ id: "PR:body", kind: "body", body, ... }])

declarations : ["visible-declaration", "visible-declaration"]   # client: null, null
invalidMarkers: ["marker requires exactly one complete visible attribution footer"]
coverage     : "partial"

# repository CI gate, imported from elizaOS/eliza@develop:scripts/check-pr-agent-attribution.mjs
evaluatePrAttribution(body).findings -> []      # PASSES
```

Deleting only the template's provenance block from the same body flips the
scorer to `machine-marker`, `client: "Claude Code"`, `invalidMarkers: []`,
`coverage: "complete"` — and would fail the CI gate.

The same verdict is produced by the previously deployed validator
(elizaOS/army@`04a50cb0`), so this is not a recent regression; it has been
dropping markers for as long as both requirements have coexisted.

## Blast radius

Every AI-assisted PR to this repository that follows the skill and the template.
The lost fields are exactly the ones the ledger uses to attribute a contribution
to a client and a skill revision, so the effect is silent: the PR still shows a
visible declaration, CI is green, and nothing reports that the marker was
discarded.

## Candidate fixes

1. **Scope the count to the footer block (preferred, validator-side).**
   `markerFooterError` already isolates the terminal footer — it locates the
   marker, walks back over the declaration lines, and requires exactly one
   terminal lane signature immediately before the marker. Counting the four
   labels within that block instead of the whole body preserves every property
   the check enforces (a complete footer, adjacent to its marker, matching the
   marker payload) while ignoring rows elsewhere in the body. Note this file
   lives in `elizaOS/army`, not here.

2. **Relabel the template rows (contributor-side workaround, no validator
   change).** `rowValue()` in `check-pr-agent-attribution.mjs` strips a leading
   `- ` and then `^[^:]+:\s*`, so a row's visible label is not load-bearing for
   the CI gate — only its `<!-- attribution-row:… -->` marker and its value are.
   Rewording the three colliding labels (for example `Agent tooling:`,
   `Skill ref:`, `Disclosure:`) satisfies both gates today: measured on the same
   body, CI findings `[]` and scorer `machine-marker` / `coverage: complete`.
   The skill-revision row must keep *some* label ending in a colon, because
   `rowValue` would otherwise strip everything up to the first colon of
   `owner/repo@sha:path` and mangle the value.

Fix 1 is the right shape — the template's labels are the natural English for
those rows, and a contributor should not have to know which words a downstream
parser reserves. Fix 2 is offered because it is available immediately and needs
nothing from the scoring repository.

I'm happy to open either PR (or both) — say which, and whether the template
change should preserve the current labels in a comment for readers.

This issue body deliberately carries a single attribution footer and no template
provenance rows, because that is the only shape that currently keeps its own
marker valid.

3f:T1133,## What happens

A real Telegram message to the production eliza-app bot on 2026-08-05 produced this, and nothing else — no reply to the sender:

```
[ERRO] Background message processing failed
       error="Identity resolve response missing userId, organizationId, or agentId"
```

Every linked connector identity on production is in exactly the state that triggers it:

| platform | linked identities | of those, org has zero agent sandboxes |
|---|---|---|
| telegram | 11 | **11** |
| whatsapp | 0 | 0 |
| phone (twilio + blooio) | 31 | **31** |

31 distinct organizations. So the shared webhook has never worked for anyone who signed up but doesn't already own an agent.

## Why

`resolveIdentity` in `packages/cloud/services/gateway-webhook/src/server-router.ts` treats a missing `agentId` as a malformed response:

```ts
if (!userId || !organizationId || !agentId) {
  throw new Error("Identity resolve response missing userId, organizationId, or agentId");
}
```

The API is right and the gateway is wrong: `internal/identity/resolve` deliberately answers **200** with `agentId: null` for someone who has a cloud account but no sandbox yet, and reserves 404 for an unknown identity or a user with no organization.

Because the function throws instead of returning, `identity` is never bound, so the `if (!identity)` onboarding branch in `webhook-handler.ts` is unreachable for these users. And the throw lands in the fire-and-forget `processMessage().catch(...)` **after** the webhook already acked 200 — Telegram will not retry, so the user gets silence rather than an error.

Two things make it worse: the dedup key is written before the background work with a 300s TTL, so re-sending the same text within five minutes is swallowed as a duplicate; and the identity cache TTL is also 300s.

## Second wall behind it

Even handing the resolved user through is not enough. The onboarding route hardcodes "no user" for every internal caller:

```ts
const internal = await requireInternalAuth(c);
if (internal instanceof Response) throw ValidationError("Invalid Authorization header");
return { authenticatedUser: null, trustedPlatformIdentity: true };
```

and `ensureElizaAppProvisioning` — the only agent creator in eliza-app, one call site in the whole repo — is gated on `!requiresLogin && session.userId && session.organizationId`. So the gateway is structurally incapable of triggering what the app triggers.

## What it should do

Same code as the app, not equivalent behaviour: a linked sender with no servable agent goes to authenticated onboarding, which provisions. A linked sender with a running agent routes to it, unchanged. An unknown sender gets anonymous onboarding, unchanged.

Two constraints that are easy to get wrong and worth writing down here:

1. The account must be resolved **server-side** from `(platform, platformUserId)`, never taken from the request body. `requireInternalAuth` is a flat shared secret with no per-service scoping, and this path reaches `launchManagedElizaAgent`, whose `launchUrl` carries a `cloudLaunchSession` redeemable with no authentication for the agent's bearer token. Discord already does it the right way — `agent-gateway-router.ts` resolves the owner itself and only then passes `authenticatedUser`.
2. The routing decision must key on "is there an agent that can actually serve this", i.e. the sandbox row **and** its `agent:<id>:server` registry key — not on `agentId != null`. The row exists the moment provisioning starts; the key only once a container has booted. Branching on the row alone answers message 1 and then goes silent again until boot, permanently if provisioning ends in `error`. And never branch on `sandbox.status`: a stopped agent is still a resolved agent, and re-onboarding one duplicates it.

## Blast radius of the fix

31 organizations provision a container and consume the $5 starter grant on their next inbound message. `checkAgentCreditGate` is the only brake and it only stops drained orgs.

Also worth stating: `ensureElizaAppProvisioning` only runs once a preferred name is captured, and name sanitisation keeps printable ASCII only. A Telegram `first_name` that is Cyrillic, CJK or emoji-only sanitises to empty, and both name-inference patterns are ASCII, so that user is asked "what should I call you?" forever. Pre-existing, out of scope here, but it should not be discovered in production.

41:Tbbf,## Post-merge regression

PR #18094 merged as `develop@112a73c8eec7b6491208e6e04d3687482b905e62` while the exact-head timezone blocker remained unresolved: https://github.com/elizaOS/eliza/pull/18094#pullrequestreview-4890015957

The four relevant blobs (`humanize.ts`, its tests, `trigger.ts`, and its tests) are identical between reviewed head `165f4331b216c48530967f44d259a8e45a8fb1d4` and the merge commit.

## Current behavior

`describeOnceAt` formats the absolute `scheduledAtIso` with process-local `Date.getHours()`, `getDay()`, and calendar constructors. `opCreate` receives the originating `Memory`, but `describeSchedule` receives only the stored trigger config and never resolves `message.content.metadata.uiTimeZone` or the agent `TIMEZONE` setting.

That differs from the canonical `CURRENT_TIME` contract, which resolves:

1. sending-client `metadata.uiTimeZone`;
2. agent `TIMEZONE`;
3. runtime-host timezone.

On a shared or dedicated Cloud agent, host time is not the sending user's time.

## Deterministic reproduction

Pinned Bun `1.3.14`, process `TZ=UTC`:

- now: `2026-08-08T12:00:00.000Z`
- scheduled instant: `2026-08-09T12:00:00.000Z`
- sending user: `America/New_York`
- observed acknowledgement phrase: `tomorrow at 12pm`
- correct user-local phrase: `tomorrow at 8am`

The assertion fails exactly:

```text
Expected: tomorrow at 8am
Received: tomorrow at 12pm
```

The committed formatter suite passes 10/10 and the focused action test passes 1/1 because both construct the target in the test process local timezone. The canonical `CURRENT_TIME` timezone-precedence suite passes 4/4, confirming that the sender-timezone contract already exists elsewhere.

## Impact

The trigger fires at the correct absolute instant, but the verified, action-owned acknowledgement tells Cloud users the wrong clock time and can also misstate the local weekday/date around timezone boundaries.

Historical note: #13509/#13524 addressed a LifeOps owner-fact timezone path, not this `TRIGGER` action acknowledgement path.

## Acceptance criteria

- Resolve the acknowledgement timezone with the canonical client → agent → host precedence.
- Format one-shot clock time, weekday, and date in that resolved IANA timezone without changing the stored `scheduledAtIso` or fire instant.
- Keep cron wording aligned with the timezone in which the scheduler evaluates it; use neutral wording if that timezone cannot be established.
- Add an action-level regression with `host=UTC`, `client=America/New_York`, and an absolute timestamp whose clock time differs.
- Cover a timezone date-boundary case and invalid client-timezone fallback.

#18079 was merged to develop as 6160885f561f2f38023d37d73315ef5929c5a4e3. Re-auditing that exact merged tree confirms the remaining blockers from its exact head b607317fcb7e726e7df29e429ba0b5f7bc83ff14. The five relevant files are byte-identical between those commits.

## Deterministic evidence at 6160885

1. JSON object keys are not sanitized.

packages/core/src/utils/well-formed.ts:142-147 recursively sanitizes each entry value, then reuses the original key. The exact merged helper produces:

    deepToWellFormedUnicode({ ["bad\uD83D"]: "ok" })
    JSON.stringify(...) === '{"bad\\ud83d":"ok"}'

2. An own __proto__ key is corrupted when any sibling changes.

The clone is a normal object and writes next[key] = sanitized. With:

    JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"marker":"kept"},"bad":"\\ud83d"}')

the input has an own __proto__ property, but the sanitized result does not; serialization becomes {"bad":"�"}. The assignment mutates the clone prototype instead of preserving the JSON member.

3. The provider boundary still does not sanitize the whole request.

- plugins/plugin-openai/models/text.ts:2029-2041 sanitizes prompt/messages and system, then appends raw tools, toolChoice, output, and providerOptions.
- plugins/plugin-anthropic/models/text.ts:1329-1350 does the same and also appends raw stopSequences.

A lone surrogate in an Anthropic stop sequence, or in an OpenAI/Anthropic tool description/schema, therefore still reaches captured request JSON as a \ud8xx escape. This contradicts the merged comment that every outgoing string is forced well-formed.

4. Surrogate-safe truncation reports the wrong dropped count.

At packages/core/src/runtime/planner-rendering.ts:79-90 and packages/core/src/runtime/planner-loop.ts:2279-2281, the marker count is computed from requested head/tail lengths before the helpers back off at surrogate boundaries. Exact repro:

    input = "💀".repeat(100) // 200 UTF-16 code units
    truncateToolResultText(input, 30)
    => "💀💀 [193 chars truncated] 💀"

The output preserves 6 code units, so 6 + 193 = 199, not 200.

## Release impact

#18028 currently points at the same merged commit 6160885 and therefore contains these defects. It should not be promoted until this issue is fixed and the release gates are green.

## Required fix/coverage

- Sanitize the complete JSON-shaped request immediately before each SDK call, including tools, tool choice, output/schema, provider options, and stop sequences.
- Sanitize object keys with a defined collision policy and preserve own JSON members such as __proto__ safely, for example with a null-prototype clone plus defineProperty.
- Compute truncation markers from the actual retained code-unit lengths.
- Add loopback wire tests for tool descriptions/schemas and Anthropic stop sequences, plus unit tests for malformed keys, __proto__, and an astral-only exact count invariant.

44:Tcb7,## Summary

`.github/workflows/gitleaks.yml:72` scopes the pull-request scan with a **two-dot** range:

```bash
RANGE_ARGS=(--log-opts "${PR_BASE_SHA}..${PR_HEAD_SHA}")
```

`github.event.pull_request.base.sha` is the base branch tip **at event time**, not the merge base. So on any branch that has merged `develop` (or was opened against an older base), `base..head` includes commits the branch merely *inherited* — and gitleaks scans files the PR never touched.

## Observed

PR #17420 failed `gitleaks` on findings in
`packages/benchmarks/swe-bench-pro/helper_code/sweap_eval_full_v2.jsonl` (lines 111, 149) — Go module checksums (`h1:` hashes out of a `go.sum`), matched by `generic-api-key`. They are content hashes of public modules, not secrets.

That file is not in the PR at all:

```
$ gh pr view 17420 --json files --jq '.files[].path' | grep swe-bench-pro
  (no output)

$ git ls-tree origin/develop packages/benchmarks/swe-bench-pro/helper_code/sweap_eval_full_v2.jsonl
  (no output — not on develop either)

$ mb=$(git merge-base origin/develop <head>)
$ git diff --name-only "$mb" <head> | grep swe-bench-pro
  (no output)
```

So a PR is blocked by a finding in a file it does not touch, that is not on the target branch, and that is not in its merge-base..head diff.

## Fix

Use a three-dot range, which git resolves to `merge-base(base, head)..head`:

```diff
           if [[ "$EVENT_NAME" == "pull_request" ]]; then
-            RANGE_ARGS=(--log-opts "${PR_BASE_SHA}..${PR_HEAD_SHA}")
+            # Three-dot: scan merge-base(base,head)..head, i.e. only what THIS
+            # PR added. `pull_request.base.sha` is the base branch tip at event
+            # time, not the merge base, so a two-dot range also scans commits the
+            # branch merely inherited by merging develop — re-flagging fixtures
+            # the PR never touched.
+            RANGE_ARGS=(--log-opts "${PR_BASE_SHA}...${PR_HEAD_SHA}")
           elif [[ -n "$BEFORE_SHA" && ... ]]; then
```

This is the same lesson the evidence gate already learned. `.github/workflows/develop-pr.yml` scopes its changed-file diff with an explicit comment:

> `# Three-dot: diff the merge-base..head, i.e. only what THIS PR changed,`
> `# not files the base branch advanced past the branch point (#16125).`

and uses `git diff --name-only --diff-filter=ACMRT "$BASE_SHA...$HEAD_SHA"`. Gitleaks is the remaining two-dot consumer of the same pair.

The `push` branches (`BEFORE_SHA..CURRENT_SHA`, and the orphan/root and tip-commit cases below) are correct as-is — this only concerns the `pull_request` arm.

## Why I did not open a PR

The change touches `.github/workflows/`, which needs a token with `workflow` scope; my pushes are refused with

```
refusing to allow an OAuth App to create or update workflow `.github/workflows/gitleaks.yml` without `workflow` scope
```

The patch above is complete and applies cleanly to current `develop`.

## Impact

Every PR whose branch has merged `develop` is exposed to false-positive secret findings from unrelated history, and the failure blocks `Develop PR Gate` since gitleaks is a required component. It also trains reviewers to wave through red gitleaks results, which is the more expensive long-term cost.

own failure message prescribes, whenever the row is written without the
template's optional label.

`rowValue()` drops a leading `Label: ` by stripping to the first colon. The
strip is unbounded, so it cannot distinguish a label's colon from one inside
the value — and `skill-revision`'s documented format,
`owner/repo@<40-hex>:path`, contains a colon by construction.

### Reproduction

Judged by `develop` at blob `a25d21a89641cacd1a5f4e128724373fceb8258b`, with
the five required rows present and only `skill-revision` varied:

```

  elizaOS/eliza@0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567:packages/skills/skills/contribute-to-eliza
  -> parsed as: packages/skills/skills/contribute-to-eliza
  -> REJECTED: "Skill revision must be owner/repo@full-commit-sha:path or `N/A - <specific reason>`."

the identical value behind the template's label
  Skill revision: elizaOS/eliza@0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567:packages/skills/skills/contribute-to-eliza
  -> ACCEPTED
```

The label is what makes it pass: it supplies the first colon and absorbs the
strip. So the gate accepts the template's spelling and rejects the documented
one, and a contributor who follows the error text instead of copying the
template hits a rule they cannot satisfy by reading it.

### Same cause, one row over

A routed model identifier may legitimately carry a colon — `MODEL_ID_RE`
already admits `:` in the model segment. Written without a label,
`bedrock/anthropic.claude-3:1` is truncated to `1`, which falls under the
two-character floor, so it is reported as a **placeholder** rather than as a
model — a second message pointing away from the cause.

### Also observed, and deliberately not fixed in the linked PR

A free-prose `ai-assistance` value containing a colon (`yes - used for:
diagnosis`) is truncated the same way and then reported as not beginning with
`yes` or `no`, when it does. That row's documented format has no colon and the
prefix there is genuine prose rather than an identifier, so the fix is a
different change with its own regression surface around the `no - <reason>`
parsing. Recording it here rather than folding it in silently.

### Fix

Filed with a fix: #17943. A label is prose and never carries the `@` or `/`
that make a prefix part of an identifier, so an identifier-shaped prefix keeps
its colon and every genuine label — including the slash-bearing
`Client / agent tooling:` — still strips exactly as before. Two tests are added
and the 18 existing ones are unchanged.

4a:T11ab,## Summary
`defaultSpawn` in plugins/plugin-cli-inference/src/claude-cli.ts (shared by both the Claude and Codex production inference paths via codex-cli-exec.ts) opens the required `/dev/null` stdin file descriptor with `openSync(opts.stdinPath, "r")` and passes the raw fd into `spawn(...)` stdio, but never closes the parent's copy of that fd. Node dups the fd into the child at spawn time; the parent's descriptor stays open forever. Every `ClaudeCli.generate()` / `CodexCli.exec()` call — i.e. every large-tier chat/route/synthesis inference turn when ELIZA_CHAT_VIA_CLI is enabled — leaks exactly one fd. On a long-running agent this monotonically grows the process fd table until it hits the OS limit and subsequent spawns/opens fail with EMFILE, taking down the inference route (and anything else needing an fd). This is the core inference data path, so the leak is unbounded in normal operation, not an edge case.

## Reproduction
```
Mechanism proven with a standalone reproduction that mirrors defaultSpawn's exact stdio handling (openSync + spawn with the fd, detached, no close):
  /tmp/fdtest.mjs: opens /dev/null via openSync, spawns a child with stdio:[fd,'pipe','pipe'], never closes fd; loops 20 times counting /proc/self/fd.
  Observed: "fds before: 21" -> "fds after 20 spawns: 42" (one fd leaked per call).
Control with the fix (closeSync(fd) after spawn), /tmp/fdtest2.mjs and fdtest3.mjs:
  Observed: "fds after 20 spawns (with closeSync): 22" (flat), and child stdin still functions — child reads "EOF:0" from /dev/null, so closing the parent copy immediately after spawn does not break the child's stdin.
Expected per the file's own contract ("`/dev/null` stdin is REQUIRED"): the fd is a per-call resource that must be released; observed: it is never closed, so N inference calls hold N open fds.
```

## Proposed fix
In defaultSpawn (plugins/plugin-cli-inference/src/claude-cli.ts), close the parent's copy of stdinFd once the child has inherited it. Since libuv dups the fd synchronously during spawn, add `try { closeSync(stdinFd); } catch {}` immediately after the `spawn(...)` call returns (import closeSync from node:fs). This releases the descriptor for both the success and error/timeout paths without touching the child's stdin (verified: child still sees /dev/null EOF). Scope is ~2 lines plus the import; both CLI variants share this spawner so a single fix covers claude-cli and codex-cli-exec. Test plan (>=10 real lines) added to __tests__/cli-inference.test.ts alongside the existing real-spawn "defaultSpawn timeout escalation" block: a test that snapshots readdirSync('/proc/self/fd').length, runs defaultSpawn against a trivial real child (process.execPath -e 'process.exit(0)') ~15 times with stdinPath '/dev/null', and asserts the post-run fd count has not grown by more than a small constant (proving no per-call leak). Gate the assertion on process.platform === 'linux' (procfs) or use a portable fd probe; the existing suite already spawns real children here so no new harness is required.

## Evidence plan
The PR will attach: (1) the new failing-before/passing-after fd-count test output from `bun run --cwd plugins/plugin-cli-inference test`; (2) a before/after /proc/self/fd count from a loop of real defaultSpawn calls showing linear growth pre-fix and flat post-fix; (3) confirmation the child stdin still receives EOF from /dev/null after the immediate close (child prints EOF marker), proving the fix does not regress the "stdin REQUIRED" behavior the file documents.

`selectReplayEvents` in `packages/agent/src/api/ws-event-replay.ts` is documented to cap replays "to the `limit` most recent so a stale cursor can never replay an unbounded burst", but any `limit <= 0` (or `NaN`) **inverts the cap into a full-buffer replay**. The clamp maps invalid limits to `cap = 0`, and `Array.slice(-0)` behaves as `slice(0)` — a full copy — so the "replay nothing" case replays everything.

## Affected code path

- `packages/agent/src/api/ws-event-replay.ts:94-102`

```ts
const cap = limit > 0 ? limit : 0;
if (cursor === null) {
  return cap >= buffer.length ? buffer.slice() : buffer.slice(-cap); // slice(-0) === slice(0)
}
...
return missing.length > cap ? missing.slice(-cap) : missing;        // same inversion
```

Both the no-cursor path and the cursor path fail open. The buffer holds up to `maxBufferedEvents` (1500) envelopes, so an inverted cap floods the client with the entire buffer instead of nothing.

## Reproduction (verified on current `develop`, commit aeae937584)

```ts
selectReplayEvents([{eventId:"evt-1"},{eventId:"evt-2"},{eventId:"evt-3"}], null, 0);
// → all three events   (expected: [])
selectReplayEvents(buffer, null, -5);
// → full buffer       (expected: [])
selectReplayEvents(buffer, 1, NaN);
// → every event past seq 1   (expected: [])
```

## Reachability

The sole production caller (`api/server.ts` WS replay) passes the constant `DEFAULT_REPLAY_LIMIT = 120`, so the inversion is not reachable over HTTP today. But `selectReplayEvents` is an exported bounding primitive with its own unit-test file, and its JSDoc states the safety contract; any future caller that wires `limit` to a query parameter or config inherits a fail-open flood instead of a bounded replay. The existing test suite never covers `limit <= 0`.

## Expected behavior

A non-positive or non-numeric limit means "replay nothing" — the safe direction for a cap whose purpose is burst prevention.

## Proposed fix direction

Return `[]` when the clamped cap is zero:

```ts
const cap = limit > 0 ? limit : 0;
if (cap === 0) return [];
```

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `limit = 0`, negative, and `NaN` return `[]` on both the no-cursor and cursor paths.
- [ ] Existing replay tests keep passing unchanged.

That guarantee only holds when billing is NOT configured. 4f:T4fd,Child of #16064 (LP3 device-integration batch, root-caused live on a Light Phone III).

## Bug

Every streamed assistant voice reply is spoken **twice**. A streaming reply is first announced to `queueAssistantSpeech` under the provisional client id (`temp-resp-*` from `useChatSend`), then re-announced with identical (or extended) text under its persisted server id.

In `packages/ui/src/hooks/useVoiceChat.ts`, `queueAssistantSpeech` treats the id flip as a brand-new assistant message and resets `assistantSpeechRef` — including `queuedSpeakablePrefix` — so the whole already-spoken reply is re-queued and played again. Heard live as the agent repeating every answer a beat later.

## Fix

When the promoted message's speakable text continues (or is a prefix of) what the previous state already queued, carry `queuedSpeakablePrefix` and `finalQueued` across the id change instead of resetting. Genuinely new messages (different text) still reset as before.

## Repro (unit)

1. `queueAssistantSpeech("temp-resp-123", text, true)` → speaks once.
2. `queueAssistantSpeech("srv-msg-456", text, true)` → **before fix**: speaks the whole reply again; **after fix**: no-op.
3. Extended-final variant: only the unspoken remainder is queued.

- Manual review: repository pruner behavior and public runner directory contract inspected.52:T577,## Problem

The benchmark CLI races `handleMessage()` against a fixed 120-second timer, but timing out does not abort the underlying message turn. It then calls `process.exit()` on every terminal path without stopping the runtime or closing the database adapter. Live Cerebras evidence from PR #17519 consequently left the trajectory row `active` after the process exited.

This creates three false signals:

- a benchmark can report timeout while the runtime keeps generating and writing;
- abrupt exit can kill tracked post-delivery work before trajectory finalization;
- the caller cannot distinguish a cleanly completed run from an abandoned database row.

## Acceptance criteria

- Remove the benchmark task timeout option and its fixed timer race from both CLI entry points.
- Give each benchmark process/server an owner `AbortSignal` and pass it into the real message service path.
- SIGINT/SIGTERM abort active work and then run normal runtime/database shutdown; no arbitrary grace timeout.
- Every post-boot return path executes `shutdownRuntime()` and avoids `process.exit()`.
- Server EOF and one-shot completion drain tracked post-delivery work before adapter close.
- Cover completion, cancellation, malformed input, and cleanup with focused tests.
- Run a live Cerebras `gemma-4-31b` task and inspect persisted trajectory state to prove it is terminal after CLI exit.

55:T1a17,## Project / Coordination

- Project board: N/A - runner-fleet reliability defect found while independently reviewing #17544.
- Parent tracker or epic: relates to #15398 (cleanup bundle) and #17534 / #17544 (control-dir protection).
- Coordination Discussion: N/A.
- Suggested lane tag: claude-code-ss251

## Scope

`packages/deploy/runner-workspace-cleanup/bin/eliza-prune-idle-runner-workspaces.sh` **fails open on a destructive path**: when it cannot determine which systemd unit owns a runner directory, it classifies that runner as *orphaned* and prunes its `_work` tree with `--allow-active`, which deliberately disables the tool's own safety guard.

The script is explicit that a miss is not an error:

```bash
# Every stage tolerates a miss: no match means orphaned, not an error.
agent_name=""
if [[ -r "${runner_dir}.runner" ]]; then
  agent_name="$(sed -n 's/.*"agentName"...' "${runner_dir}.runner" | head -1 || true)"
fi
unit=""
if [[ -n "$agent_name" ]]; then ... fi
if [[ -z "$unit" ]]; then
  echo "prune $name — no runner unit resolves to it (orphaned)"
fi
```

Tolerating a miss is right for the case the comment is defending (a genuinely deregistered runner, #15398). The defect is that **"absent" and "unreadable/unparseable" collapse into the same branch**, and that branch deletes.

### Defect 1 — unreadable or unparseable `.runner` reads as orphaned

`[[ -r ... ]]` failing, a transient I/O error, a `.runner` being rewritten during registration or a runner self-update, or any schema change to `agentName` all yield `agent_name=""` → `unit=""` → **prune with `--allow-active` on a runner that may be mid-job**. There is no distinction between "this runner does not exist" and "I could not tell".

### Defect 2 — `grep -F` substring match can resolve the wrong unit

```bash
| sed 's/^actions\.runner\.//' | grep -F -- "$agent_name" | head -1
```

`grep -F` is an unanchored substring match, so agent `runner-1` matches unit `…runner-10` first (`head -1` over `list-units` order). The script then consults **the wrong unit's** `is-active` state: if `runner-10` happens to be inactive while `runner-1` is running a job, `runner-1` is pruned as inactive. Both halves of the guard — the active check and the orphan check — are defeated by the same mismatch.

### Why this matters now

`--allow-active` is passed on this path by design (the comment explains why the tool's host-global `pgrep` guard is the wrong scope under `ProtectProc=invisible`). That is defensible **only if** the per-runner proof above is sound. Under either defect the proof is unsound and the last safety net is gone.

Observed consequences on `eliza-robot-6` this week — live jobs losing files mid-run:

- `Type Check`, job [91356781391](https://github.com/elizaOS/eliza/actions/runs/30694519256/job/91356781391) (run 30694519256, `quality-fork.yml`): died **4 s into `actions/checkout`** with `Missing file at path: /opt/actions-runners/runner-6/_work/_temp/_runner_file_commands/save_state_231cd9bf-d25a-4158-826f-06df318efd1f`; every later step including `Run typecheck` was `skipped`. The PR was never type-checked, and the red X had nothing to do with its diff.
- #17534 cites two further runs (30692175805, 30691649390) with the same signature.

#17544 removes the **blast radius** by protecting `_temp`/`_actions`/`_tool`/`_update`/`_PipelineMapping`, and it should land. It does not address the **misclassification**: after it, a live runner mistaken for orphaned still has its repository checkouts deleted mid-job. That is this issue.

Note this also falsifies an unconditional claim in `packages/deploy/runner-workspace-cleanup/README.md` ("Never interrupting a live job — two halves, both race-free").

## Required behavior

- Distinguish *absent* from *undeterminable*. Only a runner with no `.runner` at all — or one whose unit demonstrably does not exist — may be treated as orphaned.
- On an unreadable or unparseable `.runner`, **skip and count it**, do not prune. Fail closed on the destructive branch while keeping the sweep going for other runners (the `set -e` lesson from #15398 stands).
- Resolve the unit by exact match on the unit suffix, not an unanchored substring, so `runner-1` can never resolve to `runner-10`.
- Preserve current behavior for genuine orphans, and keep per-runner error isolation and the exit-code accounting.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] A runner directory whose `.runner` exists but is unreadable or unparseable is **not** pruned; it is reported and counted as undeterminable.
- [ ] A runner whose agentName is a strict prefix/substring of another runner's (`runner-1` vs `runner-10`) resolves to its own unit; a running `runner-1` is never pruned because `runner-10` is inactive.
- [ ] Genuine orphans (no `.runner`, or a unit that truly does not exist) are still pruned — the #15398 multi-orphan sweep still reports `pruned=2`.
- [ ] Both new behaviors are covered in `packages/deploy/runner-workspace-cleanup/smoke-test.sh`, driven through the **real** helper and **real** tool with only `systemctl` stubbed, matching the existing §10 pattern.
- [ ] Demonstrated red/green: with the fix reverted the new assertions fail; with it applied the whole smoke test passes. Both outputs attached.
- [ ] `README.md`'s race-freedom claim is amended to state the conditions under which it holds.

## Evidence Plan

- [ ] Screenshots or recording: N/A - shell/CI infrastructure with no rendered surface.
- [ ] Logs: full `smoke-test.sh` output before the fix (failing new assertions) and after (passing), plus the helper's sweep log showing the undeterminable runner skipped and the genuine orphan pruned in the same run.
- [ ] Real-LLM trajectories: N/A - no model, prompt, or agent behavior involved.

<!-- eliza-computer-attribution:v1 {"provider":"openai","model":"gpt-5.6-sol","client":"Codex desktop","skill_revision":"elizaOS/eliza@4b0bad53a7fd5cc0c1f0c507c849f27ebb53b1d3:packages/skills/skills/contribute-to-eliza"} -->57:T1500,## Summary

`scripts/check-pr-evidence.mjs` cannot be satisfied with a **trusted document file** by a fork contributor, because the two document-capable URL shapes it trusts are both unreachable from a fork, and the gate's own self-test fixture encodes an upload shape GitHub does not actually mint for text.

This is adjacent to but distinct from #17588 (help text omits the pasted-transcript path — that path works and is what forks must fall back to) and #16991 (head binding).

## Reproduced on `develop` (`9bdcf068b`) — all three legs

**1. Text uploads mint the untrusted `/files/` path.** Uploading `17599-verification.log` through the PR comment-box uploader mints:

```
https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30640882/17599-verification.log
```

`trustedArtifact()` recognizes only `^/user-attachments/assets/<uuid>$` (plus legacy repo assets and the `pr-evidence` release path) — `/user-attachments/files/…` returns `null`, so a row citing it reports **`blank`**, the same as if nothing were attached. GitHub's uploader mints `/assets/<uuid>` for media (png/jpg/mp4/mov/webm…) and `/files/<id>/<name>` for exactly the text formats the gate's `EVIDENCE_FILE_EXTENSIONS` set names (`.log`, `.txt`, `.json`, `.jsonl`, `.csv`, `.md`, `.html`).

**2. The release path 404s for forks.** `node scripts/pr-evidence.mjs rows <pr> --row backend-logs=<local file>` tries to upload to the `pr-evidence` release and fails for non-collaborators:

```
HTTP 404: Not Found (https://uploads.github.com/repos/elizaOS/eliza/releases/363485569/assets?label=&name=17599-bun-runtime-inventory.json)
```

Release-asset upload requires push access, so the documented `attach` flow is maintainer/fleet-only.

**3. The self-test fixture asserts a shape GitHub never mints.** The in-file self-test builds:

```
- [ ] Backend logs: [backend.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001)
```

— a **text file at an `/assets/` UUID**. Real uploads of `backend.txt` mint `/files/…`, so the fixture green-lights an upload path that does not exist, which is why this gap ships silently.

## Impact

- A fork contributor can satisfy non-visual rows only by pasting inline (`hasInlineTranscriptEvidence`) or writing `N/A`. Pasting stops working exactly where attachment matters most: PR bodies cap at 65,536 characters, and complete real artifacts — full backend logs, real-LLM trajectory JSONL (`hasSubstantiveInlineTrajectory` requires complete JSON/JSONL records inline) — routinely exceed what fits. The Definition of Done says "attach complete, real evidence"; for forks the gate structurally forbids the attachment it demands.
- Observed concretely on #17599: `backend-logs` had to ship as a pasted transcript because the real `.log` upload was classed untrusted.

## Proposed fix (I am implementing this now — PR to follow in this session)

Trust the second first-party upload shape, with tighter validation than `/assets/` gets:

1. Add `USER_ATTACHMENT_FILE_PATH_RE = ^/user-attachments/files/[0-9]+/[^/]+$` to `trustedArtifact()`, accepted **only** when `extensionFromPath()` is in `EVIDENCE_FILE_EXTENSIONS` (the filename carries a real extension here, unlike the extensionless `/assets/` UUIDs — so `.zip`/binaries stay rejected).
2. `expectedArtifactKind()` maps those to `document`; the existing byte-level document checks (readable text, `NON_REAL_DOCUMENT_RE`, size floors) still run unchanged.
3. Correct the self-test fixture to use the `/files/` shape for `backend.txt` and keep a media fixture on `/assets/`; add red tests for a `/files/` URL with a disallowed extension and for the previously-blank classification.

No new origin is trusted: `/user-attachments/files/` is the same authenticated GitHub upload surface as `/user-attachments/assets/`, with server-assigned immutable ids.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `backend-logs` row citing a real `github.com/user-attachments/files/<id>/<name>.log` upload passes the gate (verified against a live minted URL, not a synthetic one).
- [ ] `/user-attachments/files/` URLs with non-evidence extensions (e.g. `.zip`, `.exe`-style names) remain untrusted; media rows still demand real media.
- [ ] The self-test fixture no longer asserts text-at-`/assets/`; red tests cover the disallowed-extension and untrusted-shape cases.
- [ ] `node scripts/check-pr-evidence.mjs --self-test` (or the repo's equivalent invocation) and the script's test file pass; the gate's behavior for maintainer release uploads and pasted transcripts is unchanged.

## Evidence plan

- Logs: live minted `/files/` URL + `trustedArtifact()` REPL transcript before/after; full test run.
- Screenshots/video: N/A — validator policy change, no UI.
- Real-LLM trajectories: N/A — no model behavior.
- Domain artifact: the gate verdict diff (blank → ok) on a real fork-minted URL.

58:Td8b,## What is wrong

`agent_sandboxes_lifecycle_revision_trigger` fires on **every** update to the table:

```sql
CREATE TRIGGER agent_sandboxes_lifecycle_revision_trigger
BEFORE UPDATE ON "agent_sandboxes"
FOR EACH ROW
EXECUTE FUNCTION advance_agent_sandbox_lifecycle_revision();
```

No `WHEN` clause. That is what makes the revision unforgeable — a raw SQL writer cannot dodge it — and inside a single transaction it is exactly right.

**Across two transactions it means something weaker than the code assumes.** `lifecycle_revision = $expected` reads as *"did a lifecycle operation intervene?"*, but what it actually asserts is *"did anything at all touch this row?"*. Those are the same statement only if every writer to the table is a lifecycle operation, and several are not.

## The writers that are not lifecycle operations

| writer | columns it sets |
|---|---|
| `lib/services/active-billing.ts` | `billing_status`, `scheduled_shutdown_at`, `shutdown_warning_sent_at`, `updated_at` |
| `db/repositories/agent-billing.ts` | `billing_status`, `hourly_rate`, `last_billed_at`, `scheduled_shutdown_at`, `shutdown_warning_sent_at` |

The `active-billing` suspension write runs on a periodic cycle, outside the lifecycle advisory lock, gated only on `deletion_attempt_id IS NULL` — **not** on status. A row in `provisioning` is therefore reachable.

## The failure

`revokeWarmClaimSourceCredential` reads the revision in one transaction, performs out-of-band credential work, then re-fences in a second. On a miss it does not retry — `eliza-sandbox.ts` throws `Warm-claim credential finalization lost its state CAS`, which is terminal.

So a billing-cycle write landing in that window converts a **successful** warm claim into a hard provisioning failure. The window is however long the credential work takes, and the trigger for it is a periodic job that has nothing to do with the agent's lifecycle. The same broadening applies to the replacement-cleanup fences, which span docker and VPN I/O and so hold the window open for seconds.

Before the revision fence those CASes were scoped to `status` / `warm_claim_*` / `environment_revision`, all immune to a billing write. This is a regression introduced with the fence, in #17262, which I wrote.

## Fix

Narrow the trigger with a `WHEN` clause so the revision advances only when a column some CAS actually fences on changes value. That keeps the property that matters — a lifecycle write cannot dodge the counter, whatever statement performs it — while a billing write stops looking like a lifecycle event.

The column list has to be a **superset** of everything any fence reads, because under-listing reintroduces the ABA window the fence exists to close, which is worse than the current bug. So the list gets derived from the code and pinned by a test that fails when a new fenced column appears without being added to the trigger — a drift guard, not a comment asking people to remember.

Two alternatives considered and not taken: routing the billing writers through the lifecycle advisory lock couples billing to lifecycle contention for no benefit; making each call site retry turns a correctness bug into a latency bug and leaves the predicate lying.

## Not reachable from

Same-transaction fences are unaffected — the trigger still fires for them and the read cannot be stale. Only cross-transaction fences are exposed.

Found by @ss251 while reviewing #17262. Refs #17262 [stan-cloud]
59:Tf21,## Impact

**No new agent has provisioned anywhere on the fleet since 2026-08-06 ~11:41 UTC.** Every `agent_provision` job either failed (`Job timed out 3 times - max attempts reached`, 8 jobs) or is currently grinding through its retries (3 jobs). Telegram/eliza-app onboarding creates the sandbox row, then the container never arrives — the user stays on "your container is provisioning" forever.

Existing agents are unaffected (heartbeats healthy fleet-wide).

## Root cause — measured on the node, 2026-08-07 00:30–00:45 UTC

`eliza-core-prod-1` (88.99.66.168) is both a production agent node **and** the self-hosted GitHub Actions farm: 22 `actions-runner@N` services, 11 concurrent `Runner.Worker` jobs churning `elizaOS/eliza` workflows, on a SATA RAID-1.

The CI concurrency saturates the disks, and container creation — which needs journal flushes — can no longer complete inside the provisioner's 60s command timeout:

```
load average: 451.39, 356.19, 208.83          (machine sized for 16 agent containers)
/proc/pressure/io  full avg60=78.50           (the box spends ~80% of time stalled on IO)
disk util over a 4s sample: sda 78%, sdb 72%  (sustained, with ~39 MB/s writes)

366 processes in D-state:
    224  runc:[2:INIT]   flush_workqueue      <- container creates piled up
    116  runc            flush_workqueue
     10  tar             jbd2_log_do_checkpoint   cwd = /opt/actions-runners/runner-N/_work/eliza/eliza
      1  md2_raid1       md_super_wait

256 runc processes total, ages 16s → 21min — churning, not deadlocked: every
container create takes minutes instead of seconds.
```

The RAID itself is healthy (`[UU]`, no resync, no ATA errors in dmesg). The box has been in this state since yesterday morning: `systemd-journald` has been dying on its watchdog since **Aug 6 12:51** (it cannot fsync in time), right after the first provision timeout at 11:41.

## Why it kills the whole fleet, not one node

Every other node is over its declared capacity (see #17866), so the placement selector picks the only node with free slots — this one — for **every** provision:

```
[docker-node-manager] Selected node eliza-core-prod-1 (14/16 used)
[docker-sandbox] Pulling image ... Image pulled successfully        <- pull OK (11s)
[docker-sandbox] Registering ... with Steward tenant ...            <- OK
[docker-ssh] Command timed out after 60000ms on 88.99.66.168: docker ...   <- create dies
```

Each failed attempt also leaves a half-created container behind, which the replacement-cleanup reconciler then refuses to remove (`Replacement attempt label mismatch` — the guard is doing its job) or times out on, so two agents (`d6e37e91`, `f27f096d`) are stuck in a permanent cleanup loop on top of the outage.

## Remediation

Immediate (ops, needs an operator on the node):
1. Pause the runner farm on this node (`systemctl stop 'actions-runner@*'`) until IO pressure drains — in-flight CI jobs get killed and are re-runnable. Docker recovers on its own once the runc backlog flushes; the stuck `agent_provision` jobs retry automatically via the watchdog.
2. Longer term: CI runners and production agent placement should not share a spindle-backed box. Either move the farm, or fence its IO (systemd `IOWeight`/cgroup io.max), or remove this node from the placement pool.

Code-side hardening (separate PRs):
3. Per-node circuit breaker in the placement selector: a node whose docker commands repeatedly time out should be quarantined for a cooldown instead of being re-selected for every subsequent provision (it is the sole "free" node precisely when the fleet is saturated — the worst moment to hammer it).
4. The stranded label-mismatch containers need a bounded resolution path rather than an endless reconcile loop.

Related: #17866 (fleet over declared capacity — why this node is always selected).

5a:T8a5,## What happens

Meta cannot register the WhatsApp callback URL. Measured against production on 2026-08-05:

```
GET https://api.elizacloud.ai/api/eliza-app/webhook/whatsapp?hub.mode=subscribe&hub.verify_token=<token>&hub.challenge=PROBE123
→ 401 {"success":false,"code":"WEBHOOK_SIGNATURE_INVALID","error":"Invalid webhook signature"}
```

Expected is `200` with the body `PROBE123`.

## Why

Meta verifies a callback URL with a `GET` carrying `hub.mode=subscribe`, `hub.verify_token` and `hub.challenge`, **and no signature header** — there is no body to sign. That is the documented handshake.

`forwardToWebhookGateway` runs `validateLocalWebhookSignature` on every request regardless of method. For a GET, `needsBody` is false, so the body is `""`, and `verifyWhatsAppSignature` returns `false` the moment `x-hub-signature-256` is absent. Meta's challenge is refused before it is read.

The gateway on the other side already implements the handshake correctly — `GET /webhook/:project/whatsapp[/:agentId]` compares `hub.verify_token` and echoes `hub.challenge` — but Meta hits the Worker URL, so it never gets there.

## Why it matters beyond WhatsApp

There are two independent WhatsApp failures in production and they have a mandatory order. The access token has been expired since 2026-02-09 (`Session has expired on Monday, 09-Feb-26 09:00:00 PST`), but regenerating it changes nothing while the URL cannot be registered. This bug is first.

Current state: `SELECT count(*) FROM user_identities WHERE whatsapp_id IS NOT NULL` → **0**. No WhatsApp user has ever existed.

## Fix

Skip the body-signature check for exactly that handshake — WhatsApp platform, `GET`, `hub.mode=subscribe`, `hub.challenge` present — and let it proxy to the gateway, which validates the verify token. The HMAC check on an empty body proves nothing; the verify token is the credential Meta's design uses for this step. Every other WhatsApp request, including every POST, keeps the signature requirement.

## Related

The same audit found that Twilio and blooio share the symptom (`phone_message_log` empty since forever) but their configuration lives with other providers and has not been audited. Separate work.

5c:Tbdf,## What happens today

A person who has never used Eliza messages the Telegram bot. They get nothing.

`AgentGatewayRouterService.routeTelegramMessage` resolves the sender through `findByTelegramIdWithOrganization`, and when that misses it returns:

```ts
if (!owner) {
  return { handled: false, reason: "unknown_owner" };
}
```

`runOnboardingChat` is called six times in the router — twice with `platform: "discord"`, four times on the phone path. Telegram calls it zero times. The same is true of the second dead end: when the owner IS known but has no running agent, `routeTelegramMessage` returns `handled: false` with the resolver's reason and stops.

So Telegram can carry a conversation for someone who already has an agent, and drops everyone else.

## What Discord does at the same two points

`routeTelegramMessage` is structurally the twin of the Discord DM branch, minus the onboarding. Discord has exactly the two branches that are missing here:

1. **First contact** — `unknown_owner` in a DM starts an anonymous onboarding session keyed `platform:discord:<id>`, and returns `handled: true` with the reply.
2. **Known user, zero agents** — `owner_agent_not_running` with a resolved user and org and **no** `agentId` starts an authenticated session, so provisioning happens under the real account.

The `agentId` distinction is what separates "never had an agent" from "agent is stopped". A stopped agent deliberately falls through to silence rather than being re-onboarded, and that should stay true for Telegram too.

## The one design point

Discord restricts onboarding to DMs, because the reply carries a login link and posting it in a public channel hands the session to everyone reading. Telegram needs the same guard, and the information is already available: the webhook reads `chat.type` (`private` / `group` / `supergroup` / `channel`) and uses it in several places, but `routeTelegramMessage` only receives `chatId`. Passing the chat type through is part of this change, not a follow-up — without it the guard cannot be written.

## Scope

- thread the chat type from `packages/cloud/api/v1/telegram/webhook/[orgId]/route.ts` into `routeTelegramMessage`
- add the two onboarding branches to `routeTelegramMessage`, gated on a private chat, mirroring the Discord ones including the stopped-agent exclusion
- confirm the reply is delivered: the webhook already sends a canned message on the dead-end path, so the send exists — this is about routing the onboarding `replyText` into it
- tests for both branches plus the group-chat refusal, each with the mutation that turns it red

## Why now

Called out as key by the team: iMessage is being solved separately with a second phone line, and Telegram onboarding is the remaining gap on the "chat through connectors, same agent in the app" path. WhatsApp has the same hole and is likely smaller still — it is already typed as a phone provider — but it is a separate issue rather than being bundled here.

6a:T102d,## Summary

The authenticated browser continuation uses the shared onboarding chat endpoint as a provisioning status poll. Every poll omits a user message and an idempotency key, but the backend still generates, appends, and saves an assistant reply. While provisioning is pending, repeated polls therefore grow the durable onboarding transcript with duplicate status copy. When the agent becomes ready, those duplicates are returned to the UI and copied into managed-agent memory.

This affects connector continuations that reach the `PROVISIONING_CHAT` step, including Discord and Telegram once their browser continuation succeeds.

## Deterministic trace on `develop@1232c982c1594d2438a8a53b02e41a9ba86664aa`

1. `ProvisioningChatStep` always activates `useElizaAppProvisioningChat(true, onboardingSessionId)`.
2. The shared-onboarding branch POSTs once on mount, then the polling effect POSTs immediately and every 5 seconds. Those requests contain only `sessionId` and `platform`; they contain no `message` and no `idempotencyKey`:
   - [initial request](https://github.com/elizaOS/eliza/blob/1232c982c1594d2438a8a53b02e41a9ba86664aa/packages/homepage/src/lib/hooks/use-eliza-app-provisioning-chat.ts#L122-L153)
   - [immediate and interval polling](https://github.com/elizaOS/eliza/blob/1232c982c1594d2438a8a53b02e41a9ba86664aa/packages/homepage/src/lib/hooks/use-eliza-app-provisioning-chat.ts#L165-L243)
3. Each backend invocation unconditionally derives a reply, appends it as an assistant message, and saves the session:
   - [unconditional append/save](https://github.com/elizaOS/eliza/blob/1232c982c1594d2438a8a53b02e41a9ba86664aa/packages/cloud/shared/src/lib/services/eliza-app/onboarding-chat.ts#L821-L849)
4. The handoff serializes the complete history and sends it to `/api/memory/remember`; this happens when the status first becomes running, before the current poll reply is appended:
   - [whole-history serialization and remember call](https://github.com/elizaOS/eliza/blob/1232c982c1594d2438a8a53b02e41a9ba86664aa/packages/cloud/shared/src/lib/services/eliza-app/onboarding-chat.ts#L591-L636)
   - [running-state handoff](https://github.com/elizaOS/eliza/blob/1232c982c1594d2438a8a53b02e41a9ba86664aa/packages/cloud/shared/src/lib/services/eliza-app/onboarding-chat.ts#L812-L819)
5. The existing unit contract explicitly proves that a second empty/whitespace turn adds a second assistant-only history entry:
   - [empty-turn regression contract](https://github.com/elizaOS/eliza/blob/1232c982c1594d2438a8a53b02e41a9ba86664aa/packages/cloud/shared/src/lib/services/eliza-app/onboarding-chat.test.ts#L685-L700)

<!-- eliza-computer-attribution:v1 {"provider":"openai","model":"gpt-5.6-sol","client":"Codex","skill_revision":"N/A - contribute-to-eliza skill was not available"} -->6b:T4b5,## Problem\n\nPR #17873 merged with two outstanding egress findings:\n\n1. `sendReplyWithRetry` replays `message.reply()` without a Discord nonce. An ambiguous 5xx/socket failure after Discord accepted the first request can create duplicate replies, compounded by discord.js REST retries.\n2. Exhausted route or reply attempts only log and return, leaving the user with the same silent dropped-turn outcome the retry work is intended to remove.\n\n## Acceptance criteria\n\n- One logical inbound Discord message cannot create duplicate outbound replies during ambiguous transport failures. Prefer the transport library’s existing retry behavior unless a stable Discord-supported dedupe key is proven end to end.\n- Exhausted managed-route and reply-send failures produce a short, visibly distinct fallback response when delivery remains possible.\n- The fallback path is bounded and cannot recurse into the same retry helper.\n- Deterministic 4xx behavior remains fail-fast.\n- Unit tests cover ambiguous/transient failure ownership, route exhaustion, send exhaustion, and fallback failure logging.\n- Gateway Discord tests, typecheck, lint, and the required repository gates pass.\n\nRelates to #17873.6c:Ta57,## Symptom

Once an eliza-app onboarding provision ends in `error`, the messaging surface is permanently wedged for that organization. Every subsequent message replies:

> I hit a provisioning issue, `<name>`. Your control panel has the latest status, and the team can inspect it there.

forever. No retry is ever attempted, no matter how many messages are sent or how much time passes. Reproduced live: a user whose provision hard-failed during the #17880 outage cannot get a working agent by messaging again.

## Cause

`ensureElizaAppProvisioning` early-returns on the presence of **any** sandbox row, without looking at its status:

```ts
const existing = await getElizaAppProvisioningStatus(params.organizationId);
if (existing.sandbox) {
  return existing;          // <- an `error` row returns here too
}
```

`getElizaAppProvisioningStatus` takes `sandboxes[0]` from `listByOrganization`, which orders `created_at DESC` — so the newest row wins, and a fresh failure permanently shadows any older healthy row.

The early return is correct for `pending` / `provisioning` / `running` (that is the idempotency guard that stops duplicate provisioning). It is wrong for terminal states.

## Expected

A terminal sandbox state should not block a new provision from the onboarding path. Concretely, the guard should early-return only for non-terminal rows and fall through to `createAgent` + `enqueueAgentProvision` otherwise (`createAgent` already takes `reuseExistingNonTerminal: true`, so the notion of "non-terminal" already exists one layer down and should be the same predicate here).

Points needing a decision in the fix:

- **Which states are terminal for this purpose** — `error` certainly; `deletion_failed` / `stopped` need a deliberate call rather than an implicit one.
- **Retry throttling.** A node that is genuinely broken would otherwise be retried on every inbound message. A minimum interval since the last failed attempt, or reusing the placement circuit breaker from #17880, keeps a hard-down fleet from being hammered per-message.
- **What the user is told meanwhile.** The current copy points at a control panel; if onboarding now self-heals, the message should say a retry is under way rather than sending the user elsewhere.

## Workaround until fixed

Delete the errored agent from the control panel; the next message provisions a fresh one.

## Context

- #17880 — the outage that produced the errored rows (and the placement circuit breaker that reduces how often they are created).
- 8 `agent_provision` jobs hard-failed in that window; every one of those organizations is in this state right now.

6e:Tc98,## What

`packages/core/src/connectors/privacy.ts` defines the ordered connector-account privacy scale (`owner_only < team_visible < semi_public < public`) whose header documents it as the gate for "whether an account's data may surface in providers, summaries, and public posts", with a **fail-safe default to `owner_only`** when the stored value is missing or non-canonical. None of its exported contract is owned by any test:

- `rg privacyAtLeast|getAccountPrivacy|isPrivacyLevel` across all `*test*` files returns zero tests that import `packages/core/src/connectors/privacy.ts` (the only matches are unrelated mocks — see below).
- `packages/core/src/connectors/__tests__/` contains suites for `account-manager`, `attachments`, and `oauth-role`, but **no `privacy.test.ts`**.

This is a data-exposure boundary: a rank-order regression (e.g. `PRIVACY_LEVEL_RANK` entries swapped so `team_visible >= public` compares true, or the fail-safe default flipping to `semi_public`) would silently surface `owner_only` account data to non-owner audiences.

## Who observes a regression

Live consumers importing these helpers today:

- `plugins/plugin-browser/src/routes/workspace-account-gate.ts` (L10, L147) — gates browser workspace operations on `getAccountPrivacy(account)`; a default flip exposes owner-only connector accounts (Gmail etc.) in workspace tabs.
- `packages/agent/src/api/connector-account-routes.ts` (L202 write validation, L444 read gate) — the HTTP API's account read gate.

## Why existing tests do not own it

Both consumer suites substitute their own copy instead of exercising the real core module:

- `plugins/plugin-personal-assistant/src/__tests__/privacy.test.ts` L19+ **mocks `@elizaos/core`** with a hand-copied `getAccountPrivacy` — a rank regression in core passes this suite green.
- `packages/agent/src/api/connector-account-routes.test.ts` L305 mocks `isPrivacyLevel` locally.
- `plugins/plugin-browser/src/routes/__tests__/workspace-account-gate.test.ts` exercises real gate behavior but only at `owner_only` (its happy path), never the ordered-scale or fail-safe-malformed-value contract.

## Acceptance criteria

A `packages/core/src/connectors/__tests__/privacy.test.ts` suite importing the real module that pins:

1. **Ordered comparison** — `privacyAtLeast(actual, required)` across the full rank matrix (equal levels true; each strictly-lower level vs each higher required level false; both directions sampled, not just adjacent pairs).
2. **Fail-safe default** — `getAccountPrivacy` returns `owner_only` for: missing `metadata`, missing `privacy` key, `undefined`, `null`, empty string, and non-canonical strings (e.g. `"Public"`, `" public "` with case/whitespace drift, `"everyone"`) — i.e. malformed stored data can never widen visibility.
3. **Type guard exactness** — `isPrivacyLevel` accepts exactly the four canonical strings and rejects near-misses (case variants, whitespace, `toString` of non-strings), so write-path validation (`connector-account-routes.ts` L202) cannot admit values the rank lookup silently treats as `undefined`.

Tests must assert behavior at the module boundary with real inputs — no re-asserting the `PRIVACY_LEVELS` literal array.

## Evidence (verified at develop `e7b7e7c905`)

- `packages/agent/src/api/runtime-management-routes.ts:24` — `READ_ONLY_OPERATIONS = new Set([...])`, a hand-written literal of `{list, inspect_ssh}`.
- `plugins/plugin-app-control/src/actions/runtime-management.ts:41` — `CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED`, *derived* by filtering `"list"` and `"inspect_ssh"` out of the shared constant.

`rg '"list"|"inspect_ssh"' --type ts` across both packages confirms neither symbol is named in any test file at this head. The route suite exercises the partition only indirectly (an `inspect_ssh` round-trip without a proposal, and the destructive-op proposal binding).

## The failure mode

Adding a read-only operation to the shared `RUNTIME_MANAGEMENT_OPERATIONS` constant updates the plugin's derived `CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED` view automatically, while leaving the route's hand-written `READ_ONLY_OPERATIONS` literal behind — the two views of "which operations skip owner approval" silently diverge, and no test fails.

Extend the contract-pinning suite added in #29966 (`packages/shared/src/contracts/runtime-management.test.ts`, or a sibling file where the plugin constant is importable) with:

2. Optionally, a same-PR consistency assertion that `CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED ∪ exempt == RUNTIME_MANAGEMENT_OPERATIONS` so the partition stays a true partition as operations are added.

## Regression test

The pins above are the regression tests: drop `inspect_ssh` from one site or add a new read-only op to the shared constant without updating the route literal, and the suite goes red.

# Risks

Low. First-run conductor only. The deadline is an escape hatch, not a cancellation: the underlying login session is untouched, a sign-in completed after abandonment still lands via the existing auto-resume effect, and the attempt guard makes deadline-abandoned outcomes no-ops (the same settled-wave rule the deferred plugin registration watchdog documents) so a stale settle cannot mutate newer state or clobber the busy latch a newer attempt owns.

# Background

## What does this PR do?

A cloud sign-in popup that dead-ends (raw JSON on the auth callback, #19255) or is simply abandoned never settles the provision promise: nothing rejects, the `.catch` never fires, and `first-run:cloud-login-waiting` hangs forever with no recovery action.

Three pieces:

1. `armCloudLoginWaitDeadline` (`packages/ui/src/first-run/cloud-login-wait-deadline.ts`): a 90 s deadline on the visible wait, cancelled when the flow settles first.
2. `createAttemptGuard`: generation counter so outcomes of a deadline-abandoned attempt become no-ops and only the owning attempt releases the busy latch.
3. On deadline the waiting turn is replaced with a notice that carries the sign-in choice block itself: live validation showed the original cloud-oauth turn is consumed by that point, so re-seeding by id no-ops and "try again below" would have no below.

## What kind of change is this?

Bug fix (non-breaking).

# Documentation changes needed?

None.

# Testing

## Where should a reviewer start?

1. `cloud-login-wait-deadline.ts` (~90 lines) and its 5 deterministic tests (deadline fires once, cancel-before, cancel idempotent after fire, guard staleness, guard invalidate).
2. The wiring in `startCloudProvisionFlow` (`use-first-run-conductor.ts`): arm on seeding the waiting turn, cancel on settle, guarded then/catch/finally.

# Background

73:T104c,Fixes #22944. Completes the centralization #22772 started (its review named this exact gap: the fourth confinement copy in plugin-coding-tools "cannot import the new helper").

## Change

**Lift, not copy**: `packages/agent/src/api/realpath-confinement.ts` moves to `@elizaos/shared/platform/path-confinement` verbatim (null-returning fail-closed walk, errno-narrowed, J3-tagged); the three agent call sites import the shared subpath directly, no re-export shim. Deep-import only — deliberately NOT added to shared's root barrel, which browser/UI code consumes and which must not pull `node:fs`.

**plugin-coding-tools consumes it**, replacing the last fail-open walk (bare catch swallowing every errno, climbing past dangling/EACCES ancestors, lexical fallback return) and the pre-#22408 `..`-prefix `isWithin` bug (`..safe.js` false-denied inside an allowed root).

**sandbox-service policy is decided per direction, not inherited.** Entries keep BOTH spellings `{lexical, canonical|null}` and are never dropped on resolution failure — a blocklist that shrinks on error fails open, and dropping the last allow-root would silently disable the allowlist (`validatePath` skips it when the list is empty). The two matchers are deliberately asymmetric:

- **blocklist**: any-spelling × any-spelling (over-blocking is the safe direction) — pinned by an aliasing test and a post-start symlink-retarget drift test;
- **allowlist**: the CANONICAL candidate only. A symmetric matcher was tried first and the existing workspace-escape test caught it live: lexical admission re-admits a symlink whose real target escaped the root. The `?? lexical` root fallback covers an EACCES-at-init root that resolves later (pinned by a chmod test, skipped as uid 0);
- an unresolvable candidate refuses outright (`unresolvable_path`; all 8 `validatePath` callers verified to degrade the new reason to their generic branch — none switch exhaustively).

Also: deletes the exports the move orphans (`isWithinAnyRoot`, `relativeFromRoot`, `normalizeAbsolute` — zero production callers), and fixes the stale "desktop-only" comment on `core-plugins.ts` (the plugin gate excludes android/ios and store builds; this code runs in cloud dedicated agents).

## Testing

- plugin-coding-tools full suite **618/618** (38 files); packages/shared full suite 2078 passed with **3 failures identical by name on pristine develop** (`steward-session-client` — pre-existing); packages/agent batched suite 471 files with **4 failing files identical by name on pristine develop** (inbox-thread-mute, server-cors-preflight, mobile-dns, audio-redaction — pre-existing), targeted lanes for the three touched files 70/70.
- `tsc --noEmit`: coding-tools and shared clean; agent baseline byte-identical to pristine develop (5 pre-existing missing-built-plugin errors both sides).
- Mutation-checked with verified application against committed objects: lexical admission → workspace-escape test red; canonical-only root admission → EACCES test red; blocklist lexical arms removed → drift test red. Two earlier mutations that failed to bite exposed missing tests (drift, EACCES), which were added — the matrix is pinned where it is load-bearing.

## Noted, out of scope (tracked on #22944)

- `isBlockedPath` (device + `/proc/<pid>/fd` pseudo-paths) has zero production callers — the pseudo-path guard was never wired into `validatePath`, on any platform. Wiring it is a behavior change deserving its own slice; the path-utils header now states this honestly.

## Summary

Hardens the existing Google Calendar push callback path as one security boundary:

- registers no public callback route unless validated runtime webhook settings explicitly enable it
- verifies a destination-bound `gcalwh.v1` HMAC capability before service resolution or DB access
- authorizes account, grant, and audience before any notification, lease, receipt, limiter, or provisional resource-binding write
- applies independent durable principal and destination limits after authentication and authorization
- supports a bounded current/previous key ring plus explicit emergency revocation
- writes a typed immutable ingress receipt transactionally with exactly-once enqueue semantics
- preserves header/body bounds, replay suppression, conditional SQL advancement, leases, retries, and provider refetch

## Security proof

Focused tests traverse the real plugin route/runtime and PGlite production schema:

- default config has no route
- disabled, malformed, bad-signature, stale, wrong-resource, replayed, and mismatched-account callbacks execute no provider sync and create no receipt/pending state
- stateless rejects do not resolve `CalendarService`
- rate-limited authenticated callbacks return `429` before receipt/enqueue/sync
- previous-key callbacks work during rotation and fail after explicit revocation while the key remains configured
- one valid callback processes once and persists one bounded receipt with key/account/grant/calendar provenance

  repository AI workflows.

  environment.

## Safety boundaries

- The catalogue runtime and RPO scheduler have no production daemon/control-plane caller in this PR.

- Provider multipart publication is not implemented; objects use bounded immutable single PUTs.

<!-- eliza-computer-attribution:v1 {"provider":"openai","model":"gpt-5.6-sol","client":"Codex Desktop","skill_revision":"N/A - repository contribution skill was not invoked"} -->95:T49bf,## Summary

This PR consolidates the independently executable duplicate systems identified by the repository-wide audit in #30125. It establishes one executable owner for each migrated behavior, leaves host/platform policy in thin adapters, adds parity or provenance checks around compatibility paths, and preserves the boundaries that are intentionally separate (providers, connectors, auth domains, storage tenancy, platform I/O, generated output, and vendored code).

The highest-risk changes are deliberately structured around canonical kernels rather than broad package mergers:

- runtime/config contracts now execute from `@elizaos/core`, with stable `@elizaos/shared` paths acting as compatibility facades;
- dependency-light config input validation lives in shared, while agent-only defaults are applied in an explicit materialization step;
- LifeOps carve-outs use durable receipts so deleted data is not silently resurrected;
- UI and runtime local-inference selection use the same typed recommendation policy;
- Cloud/local MCP, registry, gateway routing, retry timing, frontmatter, native HTTP, screen capture, host routes, training staging, and quantization now share inward kernels with target-specific adapters;
- data-bearing or native-source duplicates that cannot be deleted safely without live or ABI evidence are guarded and surfaced rather than silently discarded.

Closes #30125.
